processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas: withered, shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: dark, twisted strips.
appearance_liquor: Sellers describe a clear orange-yellow liquor.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges.
taste_profile: Named for its aroma: sellers describe a milky note mixed with flowers and fruit, on a full body with some grip.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas. Smell the lid after each pour, since that is where the milky note is said to show.

vintage_note: Sold in small lots by spring harvest year and roast, as is usual for Wuyi famous bushes. Ask for the year, the roast and the growing area.
description:
Shi Ru Xiang, also sold as Shi Ru or Stone Milk, is a Wuyi bush named for its fragrance, in the same way that Rou Gui and Bai She Xiang are.

Its making follows the class: shaking, partial oxidation and a roast. A heavy roast could easily cover a delicate note, so ask about the fire.

Sellers write of milky aromas with flowers and fruit, and an orange-yellow, full-bodied cup. These are tasting notes, not measurements, and lots differ. Brew it hot and short.

Some sellers tie the name to Song dynasty tribute tea from Beiyuan. Treat that as a sales story unless they can show more.
history:
Chinese accounts of Wuyi tea group Shi Ru Xiang with bushes named for their aroma type. Where and when this bush was first recorded is not well documented.

Tea sellers link the name Shi Ru to a Song dynasty tribute tea, without citing a historical record, so the link remains unproven.
